ops.expect: From the North Creek Trailhead (officially the Gilbert Trailhead; ~3,660 ft, reached via Twisp River Road/FR-44 roughly 22-25 miles west of Twisp), pick up North Creek Trail #413. The first ~50 feet of tread is shared with the Twisp Pass Trail — bear right (north) to stay on North Creek Trail. The lower ~1.9 miles cross the 2018 Gilbert Fire zone: hot, shadeless standing burnt timber with no direct access to North Creek for water, so carry enough to get through this stretch. Around mile 1.9 the trail re-enters live forest and shade returns; at about mile 2.4 a roughly 6-ft boulder beside the trail gives a good view toward Reynolds Peak. At approximately mile 2, watch for an unsigned, faint mine trail splitting off the main tread and crossing North Creek — the crossing is a rustic log arrangement (about four 6-inch-diameter logs forming an 8-ft span), reported as somewhat springy and slick, and sometimes partly submerged during early-season high water (a horse ford exists nearby as an alternative). Once across, the old mine trail — a remnant of early-1900s prospecting in this basin — climbs east, fading in and out through forest and then open talus/scree as it gains the flank of Abernathy's North Ridge. Expect roughly another 1.5-2 miles and close to 2,000 ft of additional gain, on ground that starts as reasonably solid talus but grows progressively looser and scree-covered higher up, to reach a broad 7,680+ ft saddle about 0.6 mile north of the summit. Water is unreliable above the North Creek crossing, so top off there. The upper approach faces south and is essentially snow-free by early July in a normal year; a late-spring ascent on firmer, axe/crampon-friendly snow can actually make the loose talus band easier and safer to travel, at the cost of needing snow gear.
ops.value: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.

ops.expect:
The base of the roped climbing is a NOTCH on the ridge crest, and the feature that identifies it is a single conspicuous GENDARME standing alone on the ridge. The notch you want is immediately WEST of that lone gendarme. Not east of it, not the next notch along — west, with the gendarme on your east side as you stand in it.

Getting there: from the Porcupine Creek basin or the Argonaut-Colchuck col area at about 7,700 ft, angle up snow or blocky rock to gain the crest. The southeast ridge can be crossed lower at a notch around 6,750 ft, so a notch on its own does not tell you much — the gendarme does.

In cloud, work the crest until you meet a free-standing tower, then take the gap on its west side. If you are already on knife-edge ground with exposure, you have gone past the start and are on the route.
ops.value:
The climb follows the crest of the southeast ridge, which rises from the Ingalls Creek side to the southeast spire, the lowest of Argonaut's three summits. The lower pitches are blocky, lichen-covered and awkward, which is the sign you are on the ridge proper.

Low down, the ridge can be crossed at a notch near 6,750 ft between the south slope and Porcupine Basin; that crossing is a way between the two drainages, not a feature of the climb.

Above the southeast spire, two single-rope rappels or one double-rope rappel take you into the notch, and the route continues to the true summit on the west spire.

ops.expect: Descend by reversing the East Ridge: downclimb and scramble back through the gendarme and knife-edge sections to the notch just west of the lone gendarme where the roped climbing began. From the notch, parties either make two single-rope rappels or one longer double-rope rappel (two ropes tied together, or twin/half ropes) down steep snow to the glacier/snow slopes below rather than downclimbing the exposed step -- both are standard, established options, not just one. Anchors on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, or small trees — supplemented by whatever tat/fixed slings a prior party left; there is no bolted station, so carry extra webcord and be ready to build or back up an anchor. Once down to the snow/talus below the notch, downclimb into the basin and reverse the long approach: back down through Porcupine Creek basin, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back out over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. Given the length of this descent, start it with a comfortable margin of daylight.
ops.value: From the true summit, scramble back east along the summit ridge to the top of the South Gully. Its one technical step is a short, blocky rock cleft capped by a chockstone, with a fixed sling above it: rappel it or downclimb it on belay. Below that, descend the long gully and the brushy, forested slope beneath it toward Ingalls Creek, return to camp, and reverse the approach over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. The descent is long, so leave the summit with a comfortable margin of daylight.

ops.expect: THE BASE IS THE COL BETWEEN MAGIC MOUNTAIN AND HURRY-UP PEAK, gained from the Kool-Aid Lake basin, and the col is the last unambiguous feature of the day. Above it the route is route-finding rather than following a line: parties report several viable gully options through the granite benches and not all of them match the published description. SO THE TEST THAT MATTERS IS AT THE TOP, NOT THE BOTTOM, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE. YOU WILL REACH A FALSE SUMMIT. FROM IT YOU MUST DROP ABOUT 80 FT INTO A DIRTY GULLY ON THE RIGHT-HAND (EAST) SIDE, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that CORKSCREW AROUND THE EAST SIDE of the summit block, and the last 50 ft gains the true top. IF YOU HAVE NOT LOST 80 FT INTO A GULLY, THE HIGH POINT YOU ARE STANDING ON IS THE FALSE SUMMIT. THAT DESCEND-THEN-CORKSCREW SEQUENCE IS THE ROUTE'S SIGNATURE. A summit reached directly off the ridge crest with no drop and no wrap-around is the wrong one. ON THE WAY UP, THE STEEP SNOW BAND AROUND 7,100 FT IS THE POSITION CHECK: it sits between camp and the slabs, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 3 scramble. If you gained the ridge without crossing snow, look again at where you left the basin. AND DO NOT CONFUSE THE COL WITH CACHE COL. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier. The Magic-Hurry-up col is on the far side of Kool-Aid Lake and is where this climb starts. Two cols, a mile and a descent apart. The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a source describing 'the saddle between Magic and S Mountains' is describing this same col.
ops.value: THE BASE IS KOOL-AID LAKE, and above it the climb is route-finding rather than following a line. ON THE WAY UP, THE STEEP SNOW BAND AROUND 7,100 FT IS THE POSITION CHECK: it sits between camp and the granite, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 2-3 scramble. Beyond it, broken granite leads to a gully that gains the summit ridge. Several similar-looking gullies lead up; parties report that more than one of them goes, so pick the cleanest and keep checking that it tops out on the ridge. ON THE RIDGE YOU REACH A FALSE SUMMIT FIRST. The true top is a short way beyond it along the ridge, so do not turn around on the first high point. AND DO NOT CONFUSE THE BASIN WITH CACHE COL. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier; Kool-Aid Lake is about a mile beyond it and a descent below it. The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a description of S Mountain is describing this same summit.

results.evidence: LINE: the peak's encyclopedia entry (citing the regional alpine guide and the Canadian peak database) sets La Bohn Peak west of La Bohn Lakes and La Bohn Gap and gives the easiest route as the East Ridge, class 2. Three independent trip reports climb it that way: an Aug 2002 party from Necklace Valley reached La Bohn Gap by the avalanche fan and 'travelled west up easy boulder/heather slopes to the summit at 6585'; an Aug 2021 solo party from Chain Lakes reached the gap and 'followed a trail to the left' up boulders onto the ridge, then a short knife-edge ridge to the summit block, with a cliff on the north side; a Sept 2024 party from a camp beyond Opal Lake climbed about 700 ft from the gap to the summit. OSM places the gap (47.5628,-121.2417) about 600 m due east of the summit (47.5625,-121.2499). No source describes a southwest-slopes line. The row's own descent, itinerary day 2 ('follow the east ridge/face ... to the summit block') and schedule ('along the east ridge; watch the cliff band on the north side') already said so. GAP PIN: waypoint 4 'La Bohn Gap' (47.571842,-121.249746, elev 5,856) is 550 m from Opal Lake in the La Bohn Creek drainage, where USGS 3DEP gives 4,866 ft, a thousand feet below its own stated elevation; its elevation equals the OSM saddle node's ele tag (1785 m = 5,856 ft), so only the coordinate was wrong. OSM saddle node 'La Bohn Gap' 47.5627878,-121.2417305 (natural=saddle, ele 1785 m); the USGS GNIS record (feature 1521794) 47.5623345,-121.237319 (~335 m east of the OSM node); USGS 3DEP 5,856 ft at the OSM node. Moved to the OSM node, elev kept at 5,856. The pin is not a vertex of the drawn line (a 201-point sketch up the La Bohn Creek drainage that stops at ~5,070 ft short of the gap), so no vertex moves. NOT CHANGED (owner note): the row's sentence that USGS maps label the gap about two-thirds of a mile southeast of its true position (approach, climbing_route[0], variant baseFinding, gap directions) is not supported by the sources read here, since OSM and GNIS agree and all three reports treat the saddle east of the peak as the gap, but no source was found stating where the mislabel claim came from, so it is left for a separate check. distMi (gap 9.2, summit 9.6) and grade (Class 2-3) are left as they are.

results.resolution: rule 2: the row's own name, beta start, climbing_route and drawn line are the West Ridge reached by the high sidehill traverse from Easy Pass to Mesahchie Col (three independent accounts). The Fisher Creek approach (the South Rib ascent's), the crest-over-Cub-Peak itinerary (the East Ridge ascent's approach) and the 8,050 ft flat-spot / beige gully / chockstone / false-summit text (the East Ridge's) are rewritten to the West Ridge everywhere; the five pins of the other lines are removed; the drawn line already follows the traverse and is kept. c6's disagreement is resolved the same way c6 leaned (traverse, not Fisher Creek).
results.summary: The West Ridge of Mesahchie is reached by leaving the Easy Pass trail and sidehilling to a camp below Mesahchie Col, then climbing the first gully up the west ridge; the page had mixed in a Fisher Creek approach and the East Ridge's gully, chockstone and ridge-crest traverse, which are now gone, along with the five map pins that marked them.
results.evidence: THE LINE: (1) A peak route page: hike 3.6 mi to Easy Pass (6,520 ft), leave the trail west of the pass before it begins switchbacking down, an uncomfortable traverse crossing gullies and brushy slopes; for north-side routes climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col; camp in the basin below Mesahchie Col (water); camping not allowed at Easy Pass; its routes are the East Ridge and the Icefall & Couloir, the easiest route being the South Rib (reached by continuing the traverse beneath the peak). (2) A solo ascent: Easy Pass by 5am (1.5 hr from the car), faint user trail right from the pass, sidehill at 6,600-6,800 ft, one waterfall almost directly beneath Mesahchie crossed on an easy bench at 6,500 ft, snowy basin, crest of the shoulder between Katsuk and Mesahchie by 7am (two climbers camped there), crest with class 4 moves to gentler loose terrain with cairns, base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, slightly exposed slabs down to a col at the base of Mesahchie with a spectacular bivy site, then from the col across talus to the first obvious gully up the west ridge (steep class 3/4 at the bottom, broader and gentler past cairns) to the crest and the exposed ridgecrest to the summit by 9am; downclimbed the route. (3) A 2013 two-day party: traversed from Easy Pass to the west side of Mesahchie, climbed the 'crummy west gully', bivied at the 8,200 ft col between Katsuk and Mesahchie. WHAT WAS FOREIGN: a 2015 ascent titled East Ridge went up the crest over Point 7,300, below Point 7,690, the 7,450 ft saddle south of Kitling, 550 ft up Cub Peak (the row's day-1 itinerary), to the 8,050 ft flat spot at the base of the summit pyramid, dropped a few feet south into a gully, a narrower gully with a class 4 chockstone, a bench with an old rap sling and cairn, a second gully, an exposed slab, a 150 ft Class 4 headwall to the false summit and a wildly exposed traverse around its north side (the row's beta second half, baseFinding, hazards[2], descent, pro_tips[0], watch_out[1], rope_note and the three upper pins). A South Rib ascent drops to Fisher Camp and a 6,700 ft rib-step bivy (the row's approach middle, the 4-4.5 hr and 6-hr-descent figures and the Fisher Camp / turnoff pins). PINS: Fisher Camp (ground 5,163 ft) and the Fisher Creek turnoff (5,447 ft) sit on the Fisher Creek trail 400-700 m south of and 1,200+ ft below the traverse; '8,050 ft ridge shoulder' (ground 6,908 ft), 'Chockstone notch' (7,526 ft) and 'Summit ridge crest' (8,445 ft) are East Ridge features east of the summit, not on this route - all five removed; no pin for the col is added (no two sources place it). The drawn line (105 pts) sidehills at 6,660-6,720 ft ground from near Easy Pass, passes south of the peak, climbs to ~8,580 ft west of the summit and follows the crest east to the top - the West Ridge line - so it is kept. SCHEDULE: no source times this two-day plan beyond the pass (1.5 hr, two sources), so the traverse and camp items carry no time; the ~9:00/~12:00 Cub Peak items and the 2:00 PM camp time (the crest route's) are dropped, as are the day-2 6:00/6:45 items at the East Ridge's shoulder and gully; the 5:30 AM start, 8:00 AM summit, 9:15 AM and 11:00 AM are the row's own. NUMBERS NOT TOUCHED (not provably wrong, no source states them for this line): gain_ft/loss_ft 7,480, dist_km 12.1, itinerary miles/gain/hours, summit distMi 8. Bivy entries are the regional Ragged Ridge list (left as is).

ops.find: From Easy Pass, drop about 1,400-1,500 ft on the Fisher Creek Trail into the Fisher Creek valley, passing Fisher Camp (~5,100 ft) and continuing downstream roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade below Mesahchie's west/southwest flank - this is the key junction where you leave the maintained trail. Head cross-country and uphill, aiming for the drainage that comes down off Mesahchie's basin; around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall on an easy bench (last reliable water before the ridge, and the one real ford/hazard on the approach - can be slick and is worse early season or after rain). Above the crossing, ascend a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, with steep heather slopes and short cliff bands requiring some routefinding, to a shoulder around 6,700-6,800 ft below the west ridge - a common bivy/high-camp site with flat tent spots. From here, work up the ridge crest (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain leading to a col with a good bivy site.
ops.replace: Do not descend into Fisher Creek: leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down, and begin an uncomfortable cross-country sidehill traverse west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall almost directly below Mesahchie on an easy bench - the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, a common high camp with water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col at the foot of Mesahchie, which has a good bivy site.

ops.expect: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent line: downclimb the ridgecrest and southwest gully back to the col, cross the talus to the ~6,700 ft shoulder/bivy site, then pick back down through the cliff bands and heather slopes to the cross-country entry point near the waterfall crossing and back onto the Fisher Creek Trail, before climbing back over Easy Pass and dropping to the trailhead. There is no mandatory rappelling - this is a class 3-4 scramble route and most parties downclimb the entire way - but an old rap sling sits on the bench at the top of the class 4 chockstone gully, and parties uncomfortable downclimbing that chockstone step sometimes back it off with a single-rope rappel (one rope length, roughly 30-50 ft, off the existing tat/natural block anchor - bring your own rap gear and consider backing up old slings, as their age/condition is unknown) rather than downclimbing it. The heather and slab sections lower down get notably treacherous when wet (parties describe lichen/moss-covered rock and multiple slips/falls in rain), and the waterfall crossing and loose talus/scree throughout are the main ongoing hazards. Summit-to-trailhead descent time is typically around 6 hours for a fit party (about 2 hours summit to high camp, remainder back to the car).

expect.name: Easy Pass into Fisher Creek, then the south basin
expect.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side into the Fisher Creek valley, past Fisher Camp, and continues gently downstream for roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track — this is the last built tread of the day. Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage that comes down off the peak's basin. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench, the last reliable water and the one real hazard low down, since it is slick and worse after rain. Above it, work up scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700 to 6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain leading to the col.
expect.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the ridge traverse into July, and the heather and slab lower down turn treacherous when wet.
hazards: genuinely rotten rock in the summit gullies — every hold needs testing and anything knocked loose funnels down the gully onto the party
the cliffy gully-and-rib maze on the summit pyramid, where parties repeatedly get cliffed out without a track or route photos

the waterfall crossing at 6,500 ft, slick and worse after rain or with snow still around
lichen- and moss-covered rock lower down that becomes very slippery when wet
a long, exposed ridge with few bail options and real exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
expect.baseFinding: THE ROCK CHANGES COLOUR AT THE START, AND THAT IS THE TEST. The base of the climbing is a flat spot on the ridge at about 8,050 ft where the south rib meets the gully system at the foot of the summit pyramid. From that flat spot you do not climb — you step DOWN a few feet to the south, on your left, to enter the first gully. The correct gully is unmistakably BEIGE, noticeably paler than the darker rock of the ridge you walked up, and it is steep Class 3 to 4 where it starts before broadening and easing once a string of cairns appears. Follow it until it steepens again and look left for a notch: a chockstone is jammed at the top of it and pulling past that chockstone is the Class 4 move that gains a deep-cut traverse into a second gully. Immediately above the chockstone you should arrive on a flat bench carrying an old rappel sling and a large cairn — if you have climbed a gully and found no bench, no sling and no cairn, you are in the wrong one. Two other ways to know you are wrong: if the gully rock is the same colour as the ridge, and if you started climbing upward from the flat spot instead of dropping a few feet south into it first.

value.name: Easy Pass, then the sidehill traverse to Mesahchie Col
value.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. Leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down into Fisher Creek, and sidehill cross-country west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall almost directly below the peak on an easy bench; the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, the usual high camp, which has water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col.

value.baseFinding: The climbing starts at MESAHCHIE COL, the col at the foot of Mesahchie's west ridge. From the basin, the shoulder crest leads up to cairned ground; follow the cairns to the base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, and traverse slightly exposed slabs down to the col, which holds a well-built bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the FIRST obvious gully leading up the west ridge. The right gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, then enters a broader, gentler gully past a string of cairns and tops out on the ridge crest; the crest is then followed east, exposed but moderate, to the summit. Negative marker: if you reached the peak along the crest from the east and are starting from a flat spot at the foot of the summit pyramid, you are on the East Ridge, not this route.

ops.expect: Follow the crest over a series of small false points. Past it the ridge is moderate but narrow, dropping away on both sides, to the top.

results.evidence: Three independent accounts describe the same line and none reaches the summit from Headlee Pass. (1) The club route page: follow the Sunrise Mine Trail ~0.5 mi to just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, take the abandoned path / line of least resistance on the river's east side, past a house-sized boulder (3,100 ft) either cross and climb a ridge ramp SW to the 4,000 ft upper basin or continue to the ~3,700 ft basin and climb the steep gully (or slabs right of it) directly east; snow-covered slabs to the ~5,600 ft notch in the SE ridge; drop ~200 ft into the SE basin (5,400 ft), traverse right below cliffs to the first broad gully, climb it to the south ridge 250 ft below the summit; descend the climbing route. expect.name: Sunrise Mine Trail over Headlee Pass
expect.notes: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, take the trail the whole way. The first mile crosses two unbridged creeks — a log crossing, a root crossing and a more substantial ford — which need real caution in early season or after rain. Beyond them the trail climbs steadily through forest and then tightens into ever-sharper switchbacks up a narrow rocky couloir. The last quarter mile below the pass is the notorious part: steep, with tread periodically wrecked by snow and rockfall and a genuine risk from rock kicked down by parties above. Unlike the three rock routes on this peak, do NOT leave the trail at the switchback lower down.
expect.season: July to September. Snow lingers in the pass gully and on north-facing ground into July, and an ice axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
hazards: Notorious rockfall chute immediately below the pass — a helmet is worth wearing on the trail here, not just above it
Difficult ford about half a mile from the trailhead; seasonal log crossings are often washed out in high runoff
Lingering steep snow in the pass gully and on north-facing terrain into July
Loose talus and heather sidehilling above the pass with only sparse cairns
A steep gully partway up the scramble is often icy; parties commonly move onto the rock rib to its right to avoid it
expect.baseFinding: The scrambling starts at HEADLEE PASS itself — the notch where the trail finally tops out of the rockfall chute and the ground opens northward. The test that you are at the pass and not at a false top inside the chute is water: the outlet stream just beyond the pass runs strong for most of the season and is the last reliable water of the day, so if there is no stream on the far side you have not topped out yet. From the pass, leave the maintained tread and work north along and below the peak's south ridge over talus and heather benches. Cairns mark parts of the line and stop entirely higher up, so the real check is that the ground steepens continuously into rock and gully terrain rather than easing off. Negative marker: if you have left the trail lower down on open talus, following cairns northeast toward a rock tower, you are on the climbers' traverse to the towers north of the peak and you are heading for a bolted rock route, not the summit scramble.

expect.notes: An angled chimney — overhanging wall on the left above slabby rock on the right — leads to the saddle between the south peak and the true summit. results.evidence: Route page for the peak: from the creek-crossing camp ~2 mi above Park Creek Camp, continue ~2 mi to a large washout of whitish rock; the boot path to Storm King (and Goode) leaves about five minutes up-trail beyond it at a small cairn; the Thunder Creek approach crosses Park Creek Pass, descends into Park Creek and climbs back up southeast then east. THE COL SOUTHWEST OF THE TOWER IS THE BASE, AND THE TOWER ITSELF IS THE LANDMARK — a distinct rock pinnacle standing alone at the west end of the Enchantments, dividing the upper basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It is a pinnacle, not a summit on a ridge, so once you are close enough to see anything at all it is unambiguous.

WHICH SIDE OF IT YOU WANT: the SOUTHWEST col. From the col the climbing goes up a sharp ridge for about 100 ft and then traverses a few feet RIGHT onto the south face. If the ground above your col does not narrow into a sharp ridge within the first hundred feet, you are at the wrong notch.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTES, and it is a clean one because the two cols are on opposite sides:
  - Snow or Class 2 rock up to a col, sharp ridge above, traverse right onto the south face — this route.
  - A col with a STEEP SNOWFIELD to cross before you reach rock — that is the west-side line, and the snowfield is the tell.
  - Working EAST or SOUTHEAST from the pass toward light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge, with no col involved at all — that is the east face line.

ARRIVAL CONFIRMED BY THE SUMMIT ITSELF: the top of this tower is guarded by a four-foot slot you have to jump. If you have scrambled to a high point and there was no slot, you are on a subsidiary block and not on the tower.

GRADE CHECK: the hardest single move on this line is one 5.5 step-up after the Class 4 traverse. Ground that feels harder than that means you missed the traverse right and are climbing the face direct.

THE TOWER ITSELF IS THE LANDMARK — a distinct rock pinnacle standing alone at the west end of the Enchantments, dividing the upper basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It is a pinnacle, not a summit on a ridge, so once you are close enough to see anything at all it is unambiguous.

WHICH SIDE OF IT YOU WANT: the SOUTH side. From Aasgard Pass go up beside the west shore of Brynhild Lake (on snow early in the season) and swing around behind the tower to its south base. The scramble starts there: head up toward the band of white rock, pick up the ledge that leads around onto the east side, then climb the large black blocks to the top.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: this line does not go to the col southwest of the tower, and it never needs a rope. If the ground ahead of you calls for one, you have left the scramble for one of the tower's roped lines.

ARRIVAL CONFIRMED BY THE SUMMIT ITSELF: the top of this tower is guarded by a four-foot slot you have to jump. If you have scrambled to a high point and there was no slot, you are on a subsidiary block and not on the tower.

GRADE CHECK: nothing on this line is harder than Class 3. The ledge is easy but airy; take it slowly when it is wet or holds snow.
